Hey HN, this is Alexander from Hatchet (https://github.com/hatchet-dev/hatchet). We’re releasing a new open-source project today called Brickie. Brickie lets you run sandboxes in your own cloud account, primarily targeting EKS on AWS.

Sandboxes are an incredibly useful primitive for agentic applications. They serve two main functions: (1) a way for the agent to safely execute untrusted code, and (2) a durable filesystem for agents to preserve their state via snapshots.

We decided to start building this after we started on a package called `@hatchet-dev/sandbox` to integrate more directly with various sandbox providers, like E2B, Daytona, Archil, and Modal. We discovered that a lot of users had a requirement to self-host their sandbox infra for part of (or all of) their stack, due to a self-host requirement for enterprises. We searched around for the easiest way for users to self-host a sandbox stack and agent-sandbox (https://agent-sandbox.sigs.k8s.io) was the closest thing to what we had in mind: it’s a kubernetes-sigs project implementing a Kubernetes operator which spawns sandboxes as pods on supported isolation layers like Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata Containers. We learned that many platform teams were adopting this because it's a standard k8s-based deployment model and is pretty easy to customize the isolation layer, network config, etc.

However, it was missing some necessary features. brickie builds on top of the agent-sandbox project and extends it to support proper sandbox (filesystem-based) snapshots, fork, pause, and resume, all while bundling a proper orchestration and observability layer via Hatchet.

Zooming out a bit, Hatchet is an orchestration engine which supports durable execution (https://hatchet.run/blog/durable-execution). Throughout 2026, we saw high adoption from users building agents using durable workflows as the statefulness layer and execution model. But as sandboxes became more popular, something didn’t sit right with us. Sandboxes _also_ provide a durability layer, but at the filesystem level, and it became important to disambiguate what we call session state from filesystem state. I wrote a lot more about this here: https://hatchet.run/blog/agent-statefulness.

The problem with having state in multiple places is that it needs coordination, which adds complexity to your application. This was part of the motivation behind `@hatchet-dev/sandbox`: we wanted to provide an easy way to take coordinated snapshots of agent state, even when using an external sandbox provider.

So when we started looking at self-hosted sandbox options, it was critical that this architecture was supported well. We decided to support this in brickie using a pretty simple snapshotting mechanism which tars and stores snapshots in an object store (S3). This is something we’re actively working to improve and make more performant.

Brickie is early and in beta, we're looking for testers, contributors, and feedback on the deployment model. Thanks in advance!

Being a member of Capitol society in Panem is an honor not to be taken lightly, at least if you’re Drusilla Sickle, played by screen legend Glenn Close in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”

In the book, Drusilla is the cruel and vain escort for Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) and the rest of the District 12 tributes in the 50th Hunger Games, where she uses over-the-top fashion to broadcast her social status. Close worked closely with costume designer Bina Daigeler and hair, makeup and prosthetics designer Natalie MacGowan Spencer to ensure the character translated properly from Suzanne Collins’ bestselling prequel novel to the screen.

One challenge Daigeler faced was meeting Close’s request that each outfit felt connected, creating a through line that explained why Drusilla changes from one look to the next. Despite the drastic differences between each outfit, Daigeler established continuity through the character’s accessories, most notably a collection of gold medals and military-inspired epaulets that created a sense of authority.

“She wears all these medals, because somehow she thinks she is the top general of the capital,” Daigeler tells Variety.

And, not dissimilar to red-bottomed Louboutin shoes, Daigeler gave Drusilla dramatically long black nails that were painted red underneath to show her abundant wealth.

The character’s Capitol allegiance also went beyond her wardrobe, with Spencer overseeing her hair and makeup. While creating the looks, Spencer relied heavily on Collins’ source material to remain faithful to the author’s vision. Collins describes Drusilla as having implanted tabs that pull the skin on her face back, which Spencer wanted to honor. But because there wasn’t enough time each morning for an extensive prosthetics process, Spencer turned to Hollywood tape to tightly pull Close’s skin back, creating a distorted appearance. She later added tabs on the sides of Close’s face to complete the illusion, along with fake teeth that heightened Drusilla’s “scary” and “eerie” appearance.

“[Glenn] really wanted to pull it so taut that it changed all of her facial features, which it really did,” Spencer tells Variety.

Daigeler and Spencer’s shared mission: to create visuals that resonate with the franchise’s devoted fans — who “know their stuff inside out,” Spencer quips. “They’re so passionate.” When the book was released and casting announcements began rolling out, Spencer would regularly check social media to see what fans envisioned for the adaptation and what details they hoped to see on screen.

Below, Spencer and Daigeler break down the process of creating each of Drusilla’s costumes, hair and makeup, as well as the inspiration behind each look.

Drusilla makes her grand entrance at the District 12 reaping, wheeled into the frame wearing a bold yellow ensemble. The outfit is a stark contrast to the muted colors worn throughout Panem’s poorest district — the exact irony Spencer and Daigeler hoped to portray by making that the character’s brightest look in the film.

T-Mobile is getting an early start on the holiday shopping season, rolling out a slate of new deals on some of the year’s biggest smartphone releases, including Apple‘s new iPhone 18 Pro and its first-ever foldable phone, the iPhone Duo.

The wireless carrier is offering up to $1,200 off both devices with qualifying trade-ins on select plans, along with the option for eligible customers to walk away with a new phone for $0 upfront.

The offers arrive just weeks after Apple introduced its latest iPhone lineup in September, with the iPhone Duo representing the company’s most significant design departure in years.

Released Oct. 23, the iPhone Duo marks Apple’s long-awaited entry into the foldable smartphone market, joining competitors including Samsung and Google. The device features a 5.4-inch exterior screen that unfolds into a 7.6-inch display — the largest ever on an iPhone — designed for watching videos, gaming and multitasking across apps. The foldable design also makes it the thinnest iPhone Apple has released when opened. It’s currently available in Star White and Night Sky

Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro, which arrived Sept. 18, introduces Apple’s first variable-aperture camera, allowing users to adjust depth of field and lighting directly in the Camera app. The device also features a new 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera, Apple’s A20 Pro chip, an upgraded cooling system and enhanced AI capabilities through iOS 27. Available in Black, Silver, Glacier and Burgundy, the Pro starts at $1,199.

Beyond Apple’s newest releases, T-Mobile’s early holiday promotions include $830 off the iPhone 17, offers on the iPhone 16 and 17e that can cover the full device cost, and discounts on Android devices including the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Google Pixel 11 lineup and Motorola Razr. You can also get four lines right now for just $25/line and get four iPhone 17e devices “on us” when you switch.
